title: The Desperate Man (Le Désespéré)
source: Musée d'Orsay, Paris, long-term loan from Qatar Museums since 2025 (DO 2025 2), public domain. Wikimedia Commons: File:Gustave Courbet - Le Désespéré (1843).jpg (1500 x 1228 px; not re-checked on Commons, Wikimedia unreachable from the container)
caption: He grabs his hair and stares right at you. Who is he, and why did he hide this face for 30 years? #selfportrait #despair #courbet #fineart #artfacts
_verify: CORRECTION to the brief: no longer 'private collection'. Owner is Qatar Museums; on long-term loan to the Musée d'Orsay since 14 Oct 2025 (Orsay catalogue musee-orsay.fr/fr/oeuvres/272956: 'Prêt de longue durée de Qatar Museums, 2025', room 4, ground floor; QNA 14 Oct 2025 qna.org.qa; artnet news.artnet.com/art-world/gustave-courbet-desperate-man-2703520). Previously courtesy Conseil Investissement Art BNP Paribas; shown in the 2007-2008 Paris retrospective (then New York, Montpellier). First time in France in 17 years.

VERIFIED, Orsay catalogue: 'Autoportrait de l'artiste', also 'Désespoir' / 'Le Désespéré', c. 1844-1845, oil on canvas, 44 x 54 cm (landscape format); belongs to the 'têtes d'étude' tradition (showing the ability to paint emotions); tight framing, harsh light; Courbet kept it until his death (studio until 1877, then his sister Juliette, sold at Drouot 1881); signature and '41' in blood-red paint probably added when shown in Vienna in 1873, after his exile in Switzerland; first exhibited Vienna 1873, then Geneva 1877 as 'Désespoir', weeks before his death. Wikipedia EN gives 1843-1845 and 45 x 54 cm.
VERIFIED with a range, age: artnet says 24, QNA says about 25 (born 1819). Slide says 'in his mid-twenties'.
UNVERIFIED in a dedicated source but standard biography, slide 5: 'long before his scandals made him famous' (Courbet's breakthrough came at the 1849-1851 Salons). Low risk.
INTERPRETATION, flagged on slide 6: whether it shows real despair or an expression exercise is unknown (Wikipedia EN; Orsay calls it a 'tête d'étude'). 'Selfie' is our framing, not a source term.

Not used: Courbet's letter to Bruyas about a 'laughing mask' (Wikipedia EN, context unclear); reported price €50 million (Le Monde via artnet, unconfirmed); Disney Beauty and the Beast resemblance (Wikipedia, speculative).
Focus boxes estimated from the contact sheet; re-tune on the real image.

slides.headline: This man looks terrified. Who is he?
slides.sub: Gustave Courbet, The Desperate Man, c. 1843-1845

slides.headline: Paris, around 1844
slides.text: A young man grabs his hair and stares straight at you, as if something has just gone terribly wrong. But what?

slides.headline: Those eyes
slides.text: Look at the eyes. Wide open, locked on yours. The light hits hard, the frame is tight. There's nowhere to hide.

slides.headline: Hands in his hair
slides.text: His fingers dig into his hair, elbows thrown wide. And the canvas is horizontal, unusual for a portrait. It feels almost like a selfie.

slides.headline: It's the painter
slides.text: Because it is one. This is Gustave Courbet himself, in his mid-twenties, new to Paris, long before his scandals made him famous.

slides.headline: Real panic, or acting?
slides.text: Was he truly desperate? Maybe not. Young painters made 'expression heads' to prove they could paint any emotion. Nobody knows.

slides.headline: Never sold
slides.text: Meanwhile, he never let it go. He kept this face to himself, in his studio, until his death in 1877.

slides.headline: A blood-red date
slides.text: And look bottom left. The blood-red signature says '41'. Experts think he added it decades later, in 1873, backdating his younger self.

slides.headline: Still staring
slides.text: Today, on loan from Qatar, he stares out again at the Musée d'Orsay, 180 years on. Real despair, or a brilliant performance?
